column2: The scent rising from ghee smoke seems to fill the ascetic forest; seeing it, Maheshvara, may my mind always be pleased.
Explain to me this doubt, god, about the sages' dharma, lord, you who know the truth of all dharma and wealth, god of gods; tell me, Mahadeva, all I have asked as it truly is.
[Maheshvara] Come, I shall tell you the supreme dharma of sages, by which, auspicious one, sages by their own austerity attain perfection.
Hear from me, fortunate one, who know dharma, the dharma from the beginning of the foam-drinking sages, always the dharma of those who know dharma.
They always gather the fair heap of Brahma's foam, the nectar drunk by Brahma, sweet and spread in heaven.
This is the practice of dharma, the path made by those pure foam-drinkers, ascetic; hear now of the host of the Valakhilyas.
The Valakhilyas, sages perfected by austerity in the orb of the sun, who know dharma, glean grain, following the bird's way of life.
Wearing deer-skin and garments of rags and bark, free of dualities, the Valakhilya ascetics have reached the good path.
They are only the size of a thumb-joint, abiding in their own limbs, and perform austerity; their fruit of dharma is great.
They attain equality with the gods for accomplishing the gods' work, lighting all directions, their sins burned away by austerity.
Others of pure mind, devoted to compassion and dharma, the good, holy ones who move in the circle and move in the moon's world,
dwelling near the ancestors' world, glean by rule; some wash and pound with stones, and some use the teeth as mortar.
Of the soma-drinking gods and the steam-drinking ones, those who dwell near them, their senses controlled by nature, glean.
Their dharma is tending the fire, honouring ancestors and gods, and performing the five sacrifices.
This, goddess, is the sages' dharma, always practised by the twice-born who move in the circle and in the world of the gods. Hear also of the other.
In all sages' dharmas, the self must be conquered and senses mastered; desire and anger are to be conquered after that, in my view.
Tending the Agnihotra, sitting through the night of dharma, permission for the Soma sacrifice, and the fifth, the sacrificial fee.
Constant sacrifice is dharma, delight in honouring ancestors and gods, and hospitality to all with food won by gleaning.
Withdrawal from enjoyment, delight in the products of cows, sleeping on the bare ground as yoga, and feeding on leaves of vegetables.
Eating fruit and roots, wind, water, or eating moss: these are the sages' rules, by which they win an unconquered goal.
When the smoke has gone, the pestle laid aside, the embers out, the people have eaten, vessels no longer pass, and alms-time has passed,
wishing for a guest, eating what remains, delighting in truth and dharma, patient, he is joined with the sage's dharma.
One who is not stiff, not proud, not careless, not amazed, equal to friend and foe, a friend, he is the best knower of dharma.
In varied lands full of fruit, attentive, and in lands full of roots, they dwell, firm in vows.
I wish to hear the holy rule for them also, Shankara, for forest-dwellers living on their own bodies, lord of the gods.
[Maheshvara] Hear from me attentively the dharma of the forest-dwellers; having heard, goddess, be single-minded and devoted to dharma.
Hear what kind of rite is to be done by the forest-dwellers, perfected, restrained, good, who have come to live in the forest.
The thrice-daily bathing, honouring ancestors and gods, tending the Agnihotra, the Ishti, and the rule of oblation.
Gathering wild rice, eating fruit and roots, using ingudi and egg oils for oiling.
Practising yoga, perfected, avoiding desire and anger, resorting to the hero's bed, keeping the hero's posture,
the disciplined, the yoga-bearers, in summer with the five fires, and with the frog-posture, serving duly as required.
Wrapped in bark garments, dwelling in deer-skin, they should move about at the right time, by dharma and rule.
Forest-dwellers always, going about, guarding and roaming in the forest, those who live by the forest should dwell having resorted to the forest as to a teacher.
Their dharma is oblation, serving the five sacrifices, and keeping the Vedic sacrifice of the Naga-fifth.
Devotion to the eighth-day sacrifice, observing Chaturmasya, the full-moon sacrifice and the daily sacrifice.
Freed from union with wives, freed from all confusions, freed from all sins, the sages wander in the forest.
Those who always have the ladle and vessels as chief, who always take refuge in the three fires, the good, ever on the good path, go to the highest goal.
The sages, perfected, reach the greatly holy world of Brahma and the eternal moon-world, relying on the sages' dharma.
This dharma, goddess, auspicious, which forest-dwellers follow, I have set forth in its main outline, abundantly.
[Uma] Blessed one, god of gods, saluted by all beings, tell me the dharma of the host of sages in claims of perfection.
Of those perfected in claims of perfection, dwelling in the forest, living freely, with wives: how is their dharma held?
[Maheshvara] The free-living ascetics, goddess, all live with their wives; their cause is a shaved head, ochre robes, and day and night.
Thrice-daily bathing, the great oblation made by sages, concentration, standing on the good path, and practising as taught.
If they follow the dharmas told before for forest-dwellers, they gain the fruit of austerity.
Those who follow the dharma of a couple, restrained with their own wives, practise what is seen by rule, approaching at the proper season.
The dharma made by the sages is fit for them, the righteous; not other desire from wilfulness, to be followed by those who see dharma.
One who rightly gives the gift of fearlessness to all beings, his self freed from harm and anger, is joined with dharma.
One who is compassionate to all beings, whose vow is uprightness to all beings, who is the self of all beings, is joined with dharma.
Bathing in all the Vedas and uprightness to all beings are equal, or uprightness is better.
They say uprightness is dharma and crookedness is adharma; a man joined with uprightness is joined with dharma.
Uprightness dwells always in the world near the immortals; so one who desires dharma for himself should be always upright.
Patient, self-controlled, with anger conquered, dharma become, harmless, ever delighting in dharma, a man is joined with dharma.
Free of sloth, righteous, relying on the good path, the awakened one with conduct as chief is fit to become Brahman.
[Uma] God, those ascetics devoted to the ashramas, rich in austerity, by what conduct do they become radiant?
Kings and princes, poor or very rich, by what deed, blessed one, do they attain great fruit?
Having reached a steady place, anointed with divine sandal, by what deed, god, do they become forest-wanderers?
Tell me this doubt in full, god, about the auspicious practice of austerity, three-eyed destroyer of Tripura.
[Maheshvara] Self-controlled by fasting vows, harmless and truthful, the perfected rejoice after death with the gandharvas, free of ailment.
One who sleeps in the frog-posture, in place and by rule, and practises initiation, the righteous, rejoices with the nagas.
One who joyfully eats, with the deer, the tender grass dropped from the deer's mouth, being initiated, goes to Amaravati.
One who follows the vow of moss or fallen leaves, bearing the yoga of cold, always, goes to the highest goal.
One who lives on air or water or on fruit and roots, having attained lordship among yakshas, rejoices with troops of apsarases.
One who bears the fire in summer by the rite seen in the rules, having practised twelve years, becomes a king.
A sage who keeps a rule of diet for twelve years and carefully accomplishes the desert, becomes a king.
On bare ground, holding pure space on all sides, entering with joy the twelve-year initiation,
the fruits of the bare ground, they say, are vehicles, beds and houses of great value, white as the moon, O lovely one.
One restrained, restrained in food, who sustains himself and gives up his body by fasting obtains heaven.
One who sustains himself through the twelve-year initiation and gives up his body in the great ocean attains the world of Varuna.
One who sustains himself through the twelve-year initiation, breaking his feet with a stone, rejoices among the guhyakas.
Having accomplished himself by himself, free of dualities, without possessions, after twelve years of a single chosen initiation, he gains the world of heaven and rejoices with the gods.
One who sustains himself through the twelve-year initiation and, offering his body into the fire, gives it up, is honoured in the world of fire.
But the twice-born, goddess, who is rightly initiated and restrained, placing the Self in the Self, free of dualities, without possessions,
having done twelve years of a single chosen initiation, binds the fire-sticks with their kindling on his shoulder and goes uncovered.
Always on the hero's path in mind, devoted to the hero's posture, standing as a hero, he attains the hero's goal.
He goes always to Shakra's world, honoured with all desires, strewn with divine flowers, adorned with divine sandal, and the righteous one lives happily in heaven with the hosts of gods.

The hero who has gone to the hero's world, who always bears the hero's yoga, established in goodness, having given up all, initiated, restrained and pure, whoever enters the hero's path has eternal worlds.
In a vehicle moving at will, he moves as he pleases; gone to Shakra's world, the glorious one rejoices, free of ailment.
[Uma] The blessed Self-existent created the four classes before; by the ripening of what deed does a vaishya go to shudra-hood?
By what does a vaishya or a kshatriya, or a twice-born, become a kshatriya? How, god, can dharma be followed in a reversed order?
By what deed is a brahmin born in a shudra womb, and by what deed, lord, does a kshatriya reach shudra-hood?
Tell me this doubt, god, blameless lord of beings: how can the three classes, by nature, attain brahminhood here?
[Maheshvara] Brahminhood is hard to attain, goddess; it is my view that a brahmin is so by nature, and likewise a kshatriya, vaishya or shudra.
By an evil deed here a twice-born falls from his place, having come to the senior class; therefore the twice-born should guard it.
One who stands in a brahmin's dharma and lives by brahminhood, or a kshatriya or vaishya, goes to oneness with Brahman.
But one who gives up brahminhood and follows the kshatriya's dharma falls from brahminhood and is born in a kshatriya womb.
This too is another thing said by Brahma, goddess: the final spiritual teaching practised by the good who desire dharma.
A fierce man's food is censured, goddess; so are a crowd's food, the food of a shraddha-impurity, and food proclaimed, censured by the great gods of gods.
A shudra's food is censured, goddess, by the great gods of gods; what was uttered from the Grandsire's mouth is authority, in my view.
One who dies with the remains of a shudra's food in his belly, even one who keeps the fire and sacrifices, shares a shudra's fate.
By that residue of a shudra's food, a brahmin removed from the brahmin station goes to shudra-hood; there is no doubt of it.
Whose food's remains he dies with in his belly, into that very womb the brahmin goes, whose food he lives on.
One who, having won the hard-to-gain, fair state of brahminhood, despises it and eats forbidden food falls from twice-born state.
A drinker of liquor, a killer of brahmins, a petty man, a thief, one who breaks vows, the unclean, one without study, the sinful, the greedy, the cheat, the rogue,
one without vows, the husband of a low-caste woman, an eater of bastard-food, a soma-seller, a servant of the vile: such a brahmin falls from the brahmin womb.
One who defiles his teacher's bed, hates his teacher, delights in reviling his teacher, or hates Brahman, a brahmin falls from the brahmin womb.
By these deeds, goddess, and by practising their opposite good deeds, a shudra may reach brahminhood and a vaishya kshatriya-hood.
A shudra who always stands on the good path should do all the work of a shudra rightly and by rule, and serve and wait carefully on the senior classes, not downcast.
Honouring gods and the twice-born, keeping vows of hospitality to all, approaching his wife at the proper season, restrained and moderate in food,
clean, seeking clean people, eating what remains, not eating meat needlessly: a shudra attains vaishya-hood.
Truthful, not boastful, free of dualities, knowing calm, sacrificing with daily sacrifices, devoted to study, pure,
self-controlled, honouring brahmins, wishing well to all classes, keeping a householder's vow, eating twice daily,
eating what remains, master of his food, free of desire, not saying "I", tending the Agnihotra and offering by rule,
practising hospitality to all, eating what remains, guided by the mantras of the three fires, if a vaishya bears it, that vaishya is born in a pure, great kshatriya family.
That vaishya, born a kshatriya, refined from birth, initiated, intent on vows, becomes an honoured twice-born.
He gives, sacrifices with refined sacrifices with the fees given, and studies, wishing heaven, always with the three fires as his refuge.
Always extending a hand to the afflicted, protecting subjects by dharma, true, doing true deeds, he who is pleasant to behold,
with the rod of dharma, not rodless, instructing in the tasks of dharma, bound to the work, with the mark of the sixth part,
he should not follow worldly pleasures wilfully, the knower of wealth; the righteous one should always approach his wife in her season.
Fasting through all, restrained, devoted to study, pure, always sleeping in the fire-house outside and within,
showing hospitality to all, the three classes, always glad, saying that food for shudras who desire it is always ready,
he should not look for anything from self-interest or desire; he who prepares for ancestors, gods and guests,
in his own house properly attends, and lives by alms, offering the Agnihotra thrice daily by rule,
or slain facing the enemy in battle for the good of cows and brahmins, or entering what is purified by the mantra of the three fires, he becomes a twice-born.
Endowed with knowledge and wisdom, refined, a master of the Veda, a kshatriya becomes by his own deed a brahmin, righteous.
By these fruits of deeds, goddess, a shudra, though born in a lower birth and family, if endowed with the tradition and refined, becomes twice-born.
A brahmin of bad conduct, who eats all mixed food, giving up holy brahminhood, becomes like a shudra.
By pure deeds, goddess, a shudra of purified soul and conquered senses is to be served like a twice-born; so Brahma himself said.
Wherever natural good conduct stays, even in a shudra, that pure one is to be known as twice-born, in my view.
Neither birth nor rite nor learning nor lineage are the causes of twice-born status; conduct alone is the cause.
All this brahminhood in the world is established by conduct; and one who stands in conduct, fair-hipped one, attains brahminhood.
The Brahmic nature, auspicious one, is the same everywhere, in my view; where the quality-free, stainless Brahman stands, he is twice-born.
These, goddess, are the fruits of birth and indicate the shares of station, told by Brahma himself, the boon-giver, as he created beings.
A brahmin is a great field that moves in the world on foot; whatever seed one sows there, that is the farming for the next world.
He should always be moderate in food, always rely on the good path, and one who desires well-being should live passing beyond Brahma's measure.
He should study the Samhita, be a householder in his house, always devoted to study, living by giving and learning.
A brahmin who is so and who always stands on the good path, keeping the fire and studying, is fit to become Brahman.
Having attained brahminhood, it should be guarded by the self-controlled, in birth, acceptance, giving and deeds, pure-smiling one.
All this has been told to you, how a shudra may become twice-born, and how a brahmin fallen from dharma attains shudra-hood.
[Uma] By deed, mind and word, a man is always bound in three ways by bonds and snares, or is freed again.
By what conduct, what rite for the gods, what behaviour, virtues and speech do men here go to heaven?
[Maheshvara] Goddess, who know the truth of dharma and wealth, ever truthful, delighting in self-control, hear this question that benefits all beings and increases understanding.
The good, devoted to truth and dharma, free of all longing, are not bound by unrighteousness or by righteousness, their doubts cut off.
Knowing the truth of dissolution and origin, all-knowing and seeing all as the same, free of passion, men are freed from all bonds.
Those who by deed, mind and word harm nothing and are attached to nothing are not bound by their deeds.
Those who abstain from killing, of good character, compassionate, equal in hating and loving, self-controlled, are freed from bonds of action.
Those who are compassionate to all beings, trusted by all creatures, who have given up harm in their conduct, those men go to heaven.
[Maheshvara] Those who here do not speak falsely for themselves or for another, nor through jest or laughter, those men go to heaven.
Those who do not speak untruth for livelihood, for dharma, or from wilfulness, those men go to heaven.
Those who speak gentle, unobstructed, sweet words free of evil, with a welcome, those men go to heaven.
Those who do not speak bitter, harsh and cruel words, and delight in avoiding slander, the good, those men go to heaven.
Those who do not utter slander that divides friends, but speak true friendliness, those men go to heaven.
Men who always avoid spite and malice toward others, pure, equal to all beings, self-controlled, those men go to heaven.
Those who abstain from foolish prattle, avoid quarrels, and always speak gently, those men go to heaven.
Those who do not out of anger utter heart-piercing speech and speak kindly even when angry, those men go to heaven.
This is the dharma of speech, goddess, to be followed always by men, fair and of truthful virtue; falsehood is always to be avoided by the wise.
[Uma] Tell me, greatly fortunate one, god of gods, bearer of Pinaka, by what mental act a man is always bound.
[Maheshvara] Men always joined with dharma of the mind go to heaven, auspicious one; hear me tell that.
Hear also another, fair-faced one, by which a man whose mind is wrongly directed, and whose form is yet worse made, is bound.
Men who, seeing another's property left in a lonely forest, do not even in mind wish to take it, those men go to heaven.
Those who never covet another's goods lying in a lonely place, in a village or a house, those men go to heaven.
So too those who do not even in mind assault others' wives, who are wanton and alone, those men go to heaven.
Men who always treat foe and friend with an equal mind, meeting as friends, those men go to heaven.
The learned, compassionate, pure, true to their promises, content with their own wealth, those men go to heaven.
Those who are without enmity, without weariness, always devoted to a friendly mind, compassionate to all beings, those men go to heaven.
Those who are faithful, compassionate, clean, dear to clean people, always knowing dharma and adharma, those men go to heaven.
Those who, in the heap of fruit of good and bad deeds, know their ripening, goddess, those men go to heaven.
Those who are just, virtuous, always devoted to gods and the twice-born, and have attained equanimity, those men go to heaven.
These have been described by me, goddess, by the fruits of good deeds, those who go the path to heaven. What more do you wish to hear?
[Uma] Maheshvara, I have a great doubt about mortals; therefore you should explain it to me skilfully today.
By what deed does a man gain long life, lord? Or by what austerity, lord of the gods, does he gain great life?
By what deed does a man on earth become short-lived? You should tell the ripening of deeds, blameless one.
Some are of great enjoyments, some of mental enjoyments, some are low-born and others high-born.
Some men appear ill to look at, like wood; others are pleasing to look at at sight alone.
Some appear dull-witted, some wise, others of great understanding, seeing knowledge and wisdom.
Some are seen with little affliction, others with great affliction, god; you should tell me this.
[Maheshvara] Come, goddess, I shall tell you the rise of the fruit of deeds, by which all men in the mortal world enjoy their fruit.
A man who kills living beings, fierce, with a rod raised in his hand, always with the rod raised, kills hosts of creatures.
Merciless to all beings, always a cause of distress, without refuge even for insects and ants, utterly cruel,
such a man, goddess, goes to hell; but the opposite, righteous, is born handsome.
The harmful-minded goes to hell, the non-harming goes to heaven; the man gets in hell fierce and hard torment.
If he somehow rises from that hell, he gets a human birth and is born there short-lived.
A man bound by sinful deeds, delighting in harm, disliked by all beings, is born short-lived.
But one of pure birth who avoids killing living beings, with the rod laid down, rodless, never harms,
neither has it killed, nor kills, nor approves of the killer, and is affectionate to all beings as to himself,
such an eminent man, goddess, attains godhood, and joyfully enjoys pleasures that come to him.
If ever he is born in the human world, born there long-lived he prospers happily.
Thus the path of the long-lived, of good conduct and good deeds, by freedom from harming creatures, was told by Brahma.
[Maheshvara] A giver, an honourer of brahmins, giver to the wretched, blind and needy, giver of food, drink, food and clothing,
of shelters, halls, wells, watering places and lotus ponds, and all daily gifts, whatever is wished and more,
seat, bed, vehicle, wealth, jewels, houses, all crops, cows, fields and women,
the man who always gives with a very glad mind, such a one, goddess, dying, is born in the world of the gods.
Having lived there a very long time and enjoyed supreme pleasures, rejoicing with apsarases, delighting in Nandana and elsewhere,
falling from that heaven he is born among men, goddess, in a family of great enjoyments, full of wealth and grain.
There, endowed with all pleasures and joyful, a man becomes of great enjoyments, great treasures and wealthy.
These, goddess, are the beings of great enjoyments who are given to giving, long ago told by Brahma, pleasing to look on to all.
But those who are inactive, greedy, unbelievers, without giving, such men, goddess, unwise, go to hell.
If they come to human state, by the turning of time, those of little understanding are born in a family empty of wealth.
Seized by hunger and thirst, excluded from all enjoyment, hopeless of all enjoyments, they live a low livelihood.
Born in a family of few enjoyments, men devoted to few enjoyments become poor, goddess, by this deed.
Others, always stiff, proud and devoted to sin, the foolish who give no seat to one worthy of a seat,
the little-minded who give no way to one worthy of way, who give no foot-water to one worthy of foot-water,
who do not honour by rule with hospitality those worthy of the guest-offering, the little-minded who give no guest-offering or water for rinsing,
who, though a teacher has come with love, do not wish to treat him as a teacher, standing on greed that arises from pride,
who despise those worthy of respect and slight the aged: such men, goddess, all go to hell.
If those men rise from that hell, then after hosts of years they are born in a despised family.
In the families of dog-eaters, Pulkasas and other despised, senseless ones, those who dishonour teachers and elders are born.
One who is not stiff or proud, honours gods and the twice-born, is honoured by the world, a bower, humble, speaking sweetly,
who pleases all classes, is always for the good of all beings, free of hatred, pleasant-faced, gentle, kind in speech, a giver,
who is harmless to all beings by a welcome, who honours and attends with fitting courtesy first,
who gives way to one worthy of way, honours a teacher as a teacher, delights in welcoming guests and honours visitors,
Then Samvarta, turning back and tired, sat down, having reached a many-branched banyan with cool shade.
But this I ask of you, O king, bowing my head: let your meal be taken now, and then go to the hermitage.
He subdued the Nishada Ekalavya, the Kalingas, Magadhas, Gandharas, the king of Kashi, and the kings in the desert.
The greatly radiant and mighty Varchas, son of Soma, was born as Abhimanyu, the lion among men, son of Phalguna.
